summary: Young children (around ages 6–7) compare how long events last, order several events by duration, and sequence intervals on a daily timeline. Because they are not yet expected to calculate elapsed time, comparison should rest on measured or timed evidence (stopwatches, sand-timers, duration bars). A common start is needed specifically when using finishing order as the evidence of who was quicker; when starts differ, children compare the measured running length of each event instead. The central hurdle is judging duration by non-time cues: thinking the faster, further, more exciting, or later-finishing event 'took longer', or reading a later finishing clock time as a longer duration. (A stopwatch or timer started from zero at the start of each event is different: its end reading is the duration, so a bigger reading there does mean longer.) The strongest teaching separates measured duration from speed, distance, and finishing position.
misconceptions: Judges duration by speed or distance (faster/further = longer) — the time-speed-distance confusion
Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took longer', ignoring the start
Orders by how exciting or memorable an event was rather than its measured length
Treats a bigger clock-number at the end as a longer duration

activities.title: Timed race from a shared start line, then order the duration bars
steps: Run or watch two or three timed events that all begin at the same common start (for example three sand-timers started together, or three classroom activities timed with a stopwatch).
Watch each event's duration grow as a bar (or sand-timer level) and note the moment it stops.
Arrange the finished bars/timers into order from shortest to longest duration — the order is simply the bar lengths.
Explain how you decided, pointing to the measured length rather than how fast or exciting each looked.
activities.insight: How long an event lasts is read from its measured duration, not from how fast, far, or exciting it was. With a common start, whoever stopped first took the shortest time.

activities.title: Different-start challenge: 'finished last' is not 'took longest'
steps: Watch a case where one event starts late but stops last, while its measured duration (bar/timer) is actually the shortest.
Decide which event ran for the most time, and justify using the actual running time rather than who stopped last or whose finishing clock time is later.
Compare a same-start case and a different-start case side by side, and say why the start time changes what finishing order tells you.
activities.insight: Stopping last only means 'took longest' when everything started together. When starts differ, you must compare how long each event actually ran, not who finished last or whose finishing clock time is later.

activities.title: Compare and sequence from timer readings
steps: Look at two timers and decide which event took longer, explaining how the reading shows it.
Sequence three events by how long they took, using their timer readings or measured lengths.
Match each activity to its measured duration.
Place everyday intervals in order on a timeline of the day to sequence intervals of time.
activities.insight: Comparing and ordering durations can be read directly from measured values, and intervals of a day can be sequenced in order.

checkQuestion: Set comparison and ordering tasks and WATCH how the child decides: (1) Time three classroom activities (or run three sand-timers) from a shared start: 'Put these in order from the one that took the shortest time to the longest, and tell me how you decided.' (2) Two events with a COMMON start where the slower one covers less ground: 'Which took longer?' (3) A different-start case: one timer started late but stopped last — 'Which one ran for more time?' Watch whether they order by measured length or by speed, distance or finishing position.
checkAnswer: Orders the three by their measured durations; on the common-start pair names the one that ran longer regardless of speed or distance; on the different-start case reasons that stopping last doesn't mean running longest, considering how long each actually ran.
